description: Theory menu for fine perturbation. All 46 entries of the Academy of Management Journal's 'Theoretical Perspectives' submission keywords are included; the default set used for theory-targeted runs is the 20 that suit firm-level strategy research plus 7 additions (marked source 'added', 'orsc' or 'amj-topic'). Definitions are short working summaries for the generator and coder, with two canonical references each for the default set.

sources.amj: Academy of Management Journal submission keywords, Theoretical Perspectives
sources.amj-topic: Academy of Management Journal submission keywords, Topic Areas
sources.added: Added by the project because it is widely used in strategy research but absent from both keyword lists

theories.name: Resource-based view
theories.core: Firms differ in the resources and capabilities they control; resources that are valuable, rare, hard to imitate and well organized produce sustained competitive advantage.
theories.mechanism: Performance differences persist because resources are heterogeneous, imperfectly mobile and protected by isolating mechanisms.

theories.name: Dynamic capabilities
theories.core: Advantage in changing environments comes from a firm's ability to sense opportunities, seize them and reconfigure its resource base.
theories.mechanism: Higher-order routines integrate, build and reconfigure competences faster or better than rivals.

theories.name: Knowledge-based view
theories.core: Firms exist to integrate specialized knowledge, which is their most strategically important resource.
theories.mechanism: Combinative capabilities let firms integrate and transfer tacit knowledge more efficiently than markets.

theories.name: Transaction cost economics
theories.core: Firms choose governance structures (market, hybrid, hierarchy) that economize on the costs of transacting.
theories.mechanism: Asset specificity, uncertainty and frequency raise the hazards of opportunism under bounded rationality, favoring more integrated governance.

theories.name: Agency theory
theories.core: When principals delegate to agents with different goals and private information, outcomes depend on monitoring and incentive alignment.
theories.mechanism: Information asymmetry creates moral hazard and adverse selection, which contracts, monitoring and governance try to contain.

theories.name: Behavioral theory of the firm
theories.core: Boundedly rational organizations set aspirations, search when performance falls short of them, and resolve conflicting goals among coalitions.
theories.mechanism: Performance feedback relative to aspiration levels triggers problemistic search, risk taking and change; slack buffers these responses.

theories.name: Real options theory
theories.core: Strategic investments under uncertainty create rights, not obligations, to act later, so flexibility has value.
theories.mechanism: Staged, reversible commitments let firms defer, expand or abandon as uncertainty resolves; greater uncertainty raises option value.

theories.name: Resource dependence theory
theories.core: Organizations depend on external actors for critical resources and act to reduce that dependence and the uncertainty it creates.
theories.mechanism: Power follows dependence; organizations manage it through co-optation, alliances, board ties, mergers and diversification of resource sources.

theories.name: Institutional theory
theories.core: Organizations adopt structures and practices that are seen as legitimate in their environment, often independent of efficiency.
theories.mechanism: Coercive, normative and mimetic pressures produce isomorphism; conformity earns legitimacy and access to resources.

theories.name: Network theory
theories.core: An actor's ties and position in a network shape its access to information, resources and opportunities.
theories.mechanism: Weak ties and structural holes supply non-redundant information and brokerage benefits; dense closure supports trust and coordination.

theories.name: Social capital theory
theories.core: Resources embedded in relationships create value for the actors and organizations that hold them.
theories.mechanism: Structural, relational and cognitive social capital provide access, trust and shared understanding that ease exchange and combination.

theories.name: Stakeholder theory
theories.core: Firms create value through relationships with many stakeholders, not only shareholders.
theories.mechanism: Attending to stakeholder claims builds trust and cooperation that increase joint value creation; salience determines whose claims get attention.

theories.name: Industrial organization economics
theories.core: Industry structure shapes firm conduct and performance; advantage comes from positioning within that structure.
theories.mechanism: Entry barriers, concentration and buyer or supplier power determine market power and achievable margins.

theories.name: Information economics
theories.core: When parties hold different information, markets suffer adverse selection and moral hazard, and actors respond with screening, contracts and disclosure.
theories.mechanism: Information asymmetry distorts exchange; mechanisms that reveal or verify information restore efficient trade.

theories.name: Evolutionary theory / path dependence
theories.core: Firms act through routines that change by variation, selection and retention; history constrains which paths remain open.
theories.mechanism: Routines act as organizational memory; local search and increasing returns can lock firms and markets into particular paths.

theories.name: Population ecology
theories.core: Change in populations of organizations comes mainly from environmental selection rather than adaptation.
theories.mechanism: Density first legitimates and then intensifies competition within a population; structural inertia limits individual adaptation.

theories.name: Contingency theory
theories.core: There is no single best way to organize; performance depends on the fit between organizational design and contingencies such as environment, technology and size.
theories.mechanism: Fit between structure and contingencies raises performance; misfit lowers it until the organization adjusts.

theories.name: Innovation diffusion theory
theories.core: Innovations spread through social systems over time via communication channels; adoption depends on the innovation's attributes and adopters' positions.
theories.mechanism: Social contagion and word of mouth drive adoption along an S-shaped curve, moderated by observability and relative advantage.

theories.name: Organizational ambidexterity
theories.core: Long-run performance requires balancing exploration of new possibilities with exploitation of existing capabilities.
theories.mechanism: Structural or contextual separation lets organizations pursue exploration and exploitation without one crowding out the other.

theories.name: Information processing theory
theories.core: Organizations must match their capacity to process information to the uncertainty of their tasks and environment.
theories.mechanism: Design choices such as lateral relations, slack and vertical information systems either add processing capacity or reduce the need for it.

theories.name: Attention-based view
theories.core: Firm behavior results from how decision makers' limited attention is focused, situated and channeled by organizational structures.
theories.mechanism: Attention structures determine which issues and answers get noticed and acted on; salience drives allocation of effort and resources.

theories.name: Signaling theory
theories.core: When one party knows more than another, observable and costly signals can credibly convey unobservable quality.
theories.mechanism: Signal cost, observability and consistency let receivers infer quality and reduce information asymmetry.

theories.name: Upper echelons theory
theories.core: Organizational outcomes reflect the experiences, values and cognitive bases of top executives.
theories.mechanism: Executives filter and interpret information through their backgrounds; managerial discretion strengthens the link to strategic choices.

theories.name: Competitive dynamics
theories.core: Performance depends on the sequence of competitive actions firms take and how rivals respond.
theories.mechanism: Rivals' awareness, motivation and capability (AMC) determine whether and how they respond to an action.

theories.name: Organizational learning
theories.core: Organizations learn from experience by encoding inferences into routines, which changes their performance over time.
theories.mechanism: Accumulated experience, feedback and knowledge transfer improve performance along learning curves; absorptive capacity conditions learning from outside.

theories.name: Status theory
theories.core: An actor's position in a social hierarchy of deference shapes how others judge its quality, especially when quality is uncertain.
theories.mechanism: Status acts as a signal of quality, and affiliations transfer status between actors.

theories.name: Organizational reputation
theories.core: Audiences' collective perceptions of an organization's quality and prominence shape their expectations and behavior toward it.
theories.mechanism: Perceived quality and prominence reduce audiences' uncertainty and attract support, customers and resources.

theories.name: Actor-network theory
theories.core: Human and non-human actors become linked in networks through translation, and organizing is the outcome of these associations.

theories.name: Affect theory
theories.core: Emotions and moods shape how people perceive, decide and behave at work.

theories.name: Behavioral decision theory
theories.core: Judgment and choice depart systematically from rational models because of heuristics and biases.

theories.name: Complexity theory
theories.core: Organizations are complex adaptive systems in which interdependencies produce nonlinear, emergent outcomes.

theories.name: Communication as constitutive of organizations (CCO)
theories.core: Organizations are brought into being and sustained through communication.

theories.name: Configurational theory
theories.core: Performance comes from coherent configurations of multiple organizational attributes rather than from single factors.

theories.name: Critical theory
theories.core: Organizations reproduce power and domination, and research should expose and challenge them.

theories.name: Equity theory
theories.core: People compare their input-outcome ratios with others', and perceived inequity motivates them to restore fairness.

theories.name: Goal-setting theory
theories.core: Specific, difficult goals lead to higher performance than vague or easy goals.

theories.name: Human capital theory
theories.core: Investments in people's skills and knowledge raise productivity; firm-specific human capital can be a source of advantage.

theories.name: Leadership theories
theories.core: Leaders influence followers' motivation, behavior and performance through their traits, behaviors and relationships.

theories.name: Modularity theory
theories.core: Decomposing systems into modules with standardized interfaces shapes innovation, industry structure and organizational design.

theories.name: Natural-resource-based view
theories.core: Capabilities for environmental sustainability can be sources of competitive advantage.

theories.name: Paradox theory and dialectics
theories.core: Organizations face persistent contradictory demands that are better managed by accepting both sides than by choosing one.

theories.name: Philosophy of science and/or sociology of knowledge
theories.core: How knowledge claims are produced, justified and accepted.

theories.name: Practice theory
theories.core: Organizing consists of recurrent, situated practices that people enact.

theories.name: Prospect theory
theories.core: Decisions under risk depend on gains and losses relative to a reference point, with losses weighted more than gains.

theories.name: Process theories
theories.core: Outcomes are explained by the sequence of events and activities through which they unfold over time.

theories.name: Social cognitive theory
theories.core: People learn by observing others, and self-efficacy shapes their effort and persistence.

theories.name: Social exchange theory
theories.core: Relationships are built on reciprocal exchanges that create obligations and trust.

theories.name: Social identity theory
theories.core: People define themselves through group memberships, which shapes in-group favoritism and intergroup behavior.

theories.name: Social movement and collective action theories
theories.core: Collective action depends on mobilizing structures, framing and political opportunities.

theories.name: Social practice theories
theories.core: Social life is composed of practices that carry shared understandings, rules and materials.

theories.name: Structuration theory
theories.core: Social structure and human agency produce and reproduce each other.

theories.name: Systems theory
theories.core: Organizations are open systems that exchange resources and information with their environments.

theories.name: Technology acceptance theory
theories.core: Perceived usefulness and ease of use drive people's intentions to adopt and use a technology.
